title: Transition Without the Curriculum Is Just Administration
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt argues that primary-to-secondary transition, despite genuine care and effort, systematically fails pupils because it was designed to transfer administrative data — attendance, SEND notes, pastoral flags — rather than curriculum depth. Using an example school where challenging texts sit at the centre of the wider curriculum and generate 'Curiosity Sparks' that drive vocabulary and inquiry work across subjects, she argues that unless secondary teachers know specifically what those pupils have already read, discussed, and mastered, Year 7 becomes an 'inadvertent reset point' where prior intellectual work quietly stops counting. Myatt is careful to specify that fixing this doesn't require new paperwork or spreadsheets, but 'professional curiosity' — secondary teachers reading primary curriculum plans, heads of department visiting Year 5 and 6 classrooms — and insists the traffic must run both directions, with primary teachers also understanding where the curriculum is heading so they can build toward it rather than merely finishing at an arbitrary point. Her sharpest reframe treats curriculum transition not as an administrative add-on to 'real' curriculum work but as curriculum thinking itself, closing with a pointed alternative to the standard transition question: not what data is needed on incoming pupils, but what those pupils have already been invited to know and think about.
points: Myatt's diagnosis that transition systems were 'designed to transfer administrative data rather than curriculum depth' identifies a structural design flaw, not a lack of effort or goodwill, explaining why even well-resourced transition programs can still underestimate incoming students.

Her insistence that fixing this requires 'professional curiosity' — teachers reading each other's curriculum plans and visiting each other's classrooms — rather than new data systems reframes the solution as relational and low-cost rather than bureaucratic.

The reframed transition question — not 'what data do we need on these pupils' but 'what have they already been invited to know and think about, and what are we going to do with that next' — gives schools a concrete, curriculum-first alternative to purely administrative handover documents.
quotes: there's another question that seems to receive far less attention: 'What are pupils actually bringing with them from the curriculum?'
These books weren't decorative additions or topic wallpaper; the learning stemmed directly from them.
Too often, Year 7 becomes an inadvertent reset point. Gradually, the unspoken message pupils receive is that the intellectual work they did before does not quite count here.
Nobody intends this; it happens because our transition systems have traditionally been designed to transfer administrative data rather than curriculum depth.
When we underestimate what pupils have already encountered, we do not merely waste time: we lower the intellectual temperature.
The curriculum is one of the most powerful forms of entitlement we have, which means transition work is not peripheral to curriculum thinking. It is curriculum thinking.

Perhaps the most productive transition question we can ask is not what data we need on these pupils, but what they have already been invited to know and think about, and what we are going to do with that next.
